{"id": "134cdc61-cfdb-435a-b0bd-5a395a164a12", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_8OT8oGFimkEU6uVl4ZpdkZ", "content": "[{'text': '\\r\\n\\r\\n# VPN and Direct Connect Redundancy Patterns\\r\\n\\r\\nThis document captures route preference behavior for VPN and DX redundancy designs with VGW. Use this knowledge when advising on active/active, active/passive, and failover architectures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Reference Documentation\\r\\n\\r\\n- [AWS Site-to-Site VPN routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPNRoutingTypes.html)\\r\\n- [Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html)\\r\\n- [DX Resiliency Recommendations](https://aws.amazon.com/directconnect/resiliency-recommendation/)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Assumptions\\r\\n\\r\\n- Customer\\'s network does not overlap with VPC CIDR\\r\\n- Customer Gateway (CGW) device is configured to handle asymmetric routing\\r\\n- Static VPN tunnels are Route-Based only (not Policy-Based)\\r\\n- Customer advertises the same on-prem routes through all redundant connections (DX and VPN)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Key Behavior: VGW Does NOT Support ECMP\\r\\n\\r\\nVGW does **not** support Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing (ECMP). Return traffic from VPC to on-prem always takes a **single tunnel/path** \u2014 the \"Preferred Tunnel.\" This is a fundamental constraint that affects all redundancy designs.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Part 1: Redundancy Only on AWS End\\r\\n\\r\\n### VPN Connection \u2014 2 Active Tunnels (Static)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Customers can have static route-based tunnels in Active/Active mode\\r\\n- **Customer \u2192 VPC:** Can load balance (equal route metrics) or prefer one tunnel (unequal metrics)\\r\\n- **VPC \u2192 Customer:** Always takes a single tunnel (Preferred Tunnel) \u2014 VGW does not support ECMP\\r\\n\\r\\n- Customers can have BGP tunnels in Active/Active mode\\r\\n- **Customer \u2192 VPC:** Load balance (equal LP) or prefer one (unequal LP)\\r\\n- **VPC \u2192 Customer:** Always a single tunnel. Customer can influence by:\\r\\n  - Advertising **lower AS-path** to VGW over the desired tunnel\\r\\n  - Advertising **lower MED** to VGW over the desired tunnel\\r\\n\\r\\n### DX Connection with Backup VPN\\r\\n\\r\\n- DX is **always preferred over VPN** for return traffic to the same on-prem subnet\\r\\n- Customer must ensure on-prem traffic is sent over DX when both are UP\\r\\n- Attempting to prefer VPN over DX will cause asymmetric routing (VGW always returns via DX)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2 DX Connections (Same VGW)\\r\\n\\r\\n- 2 private VIFs to the same VGW over 2 DX connections\\r\\n- **Active/Active:** Equal LP + AS-path on CGW \u2192 return traffic is flow-hashed across both DX connections\\r\\n- **Active/Passive:** Unequal LP + AS-path \u2192 customer-to-VPC uses higher LP; VPC-to-customer uses lower AS-path\\r\\n\\r\\n**\u26a0\ufe0f ECMP only works when both DX connections terminate at the SAME DX location:**\\r\\n- Same location (e.g., both at Equinix DC, Ashburn) \u2192 flow-hashed (ECMP)\\r\\n- Different locations in same region (e.g., Equinix DC Ashburn + CoreSite NYC) \u2192 **single path only**\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Part 2: Redundancy on AWS and Customer Ends\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2 VPN Connections from 2 CGW Devices (Recommended Design)\\r\\n\\r\\n- 2 BGP VPN connections (4 active tunnels) to same VGW from different on-prem CGW devices\\r\\n- **Recommended:** Use higher LP + lower AS-path on preferred VPN connection to avoid routing issues\\r\\n- **Customer \u2192 VPC:** Traffic uses tunnel(s) with higher LP\\r\\n- **VPC \u2192 Customer:** Single tunnel (Preferred Tunnel). Customer influences via lower AS-path on desired connection.\\r\\n\\r\\n### DX + Backup VPN from 2 CGW Devices\\r\\n\\r\\n- DX and VPN from different on-prem CGW devices\\r\\n- When both UP: customer must ensure on-prem traffic goes over DX only\\r\\n- **VPC \u2192 Customer:** Always sent over DX (DX always preferred over VPN by VGW)\\r\\n- Design works correctly as active/passive (DX active, VPN passive)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2 DX Connections from 2 CGW Devices\\r\\n\\r\\n- 2 DX connections from different on-prem CGW devices, 2 private VIFs to same VGW\\r\\n- **Active/Active:** Equal LP + AS-path \u2192 flow-hashed return traffic\\r\\n- **Active/Passive:** Unequal LP + AS-path \u2192 deterministic path preference\\r\\n\\r\\n**Same ECMP caveat applies:** Flow-hashing only works when both DX connections are at the same DX location. Different locations \u2192 single path selected.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Part 3: Designs That Cause Routing Issues\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c 2 Static VPN Connections from 2 CGW Devices\\r\\n\\r\\n- VPC \u2192 Customer always traverses single tunnel (Preferred Tunnel)\\r\\n- If customer sends traffic on CGW 2, return may come back on CGW 1 \u2192 **asymmetric routing**\\r\\n- Only works if CGW devices have synchronization (ECMP) and accept asymmetric traffic\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c 2 BGP VPN Connections with Same LP and AS-Path from 2 CGW Devices\\r\\n\\r\\n- Same problem as static: VPC \u2192 Customer takes single tunnel, may not match inbound path\\r\\n- **Fix:** Use unequal LP + AS-path to prefer one VPN connection over the other\\r\\n- Or ensure CGW devices handle asymmetric routing\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c DX + VPN \u2014 Attempting to Prefer VPN Over DX\\r\\n\\r\\n- If customer tries to prefer VPN over DX, return traffic (VPC \u2192 on-prem) STILL goes over DX\\r\\n- VGW always prefers DX over VPN regardless of BGP attributes\\r\\n- **Result:** Asymmetric routing \u2014 customer sends via VPN, AWS returns via DX\\r\\n- This is true whether using same CGW device or different CGW devices\\r\\n- **Fix:** Advertise more-specific routes on VPN \u2014 longest prefix match wins before attachment-type preference, so a /24 via VPN will be preferred over a /16 via DX for matching traffic\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c 2 VPN Connections from 2 CGW Devices with Different ASNs\\r\\n\\r\\n- 2 BGP VPN connections from 2 data centers (different ASNs) advertising same networks\\r\\n- VPC \u2192 Customer: single tunnel, may not match inbound path \u2192 asymmetric\\r\\n- **Fix:** Use unequal AS-path values to prefer one VPN connection\\r\\n- Cannot achieve ECMP across different ASNs\\r\\n\\r\\n### \u274c DX + VPN from 2 CGW Devices with Different ASNs\\r\\n\\r\\n- If customer sends traffic over VPN, return goes over DX (DX always wins)\\r\\n- **Must avoid using same networks in multiple datacenters** to prevent routing issues\\r\\n- Or accept that DX is always the return path regardless of inbound path\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Summary: Route Preference Rules at VGW\\r\\n\\r\\n| Traffic Direction | Rule |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| VPC \u2192 On-prem (same prefix) | DX **always** preferred over VPN |\\r\\n| VPC \u2192 On-prem (VPN only) | Single tunnel \u2014 lowest AS-path or MED, no ECMP |\\r\\n| VPC \u2192 On-prem (2 DX, same location) | Flow-hashed (ECMP) |\\r\\n| VPC \u2192 On-prem (2 DX, different locations) | Single path |\\r\\n| On-prem \u2192 VPC (VPN) | Customer controls via LP (higher wins) |\\r\\n| On-prem \u2192 VPC (DX) | Customer controls via LP (higher wins) |\\r\\n| On-prem \u2192 VPC (DX + VPN both UP) | Customer must direct to DX |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Key Takeaways for Customer Guidance\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **VGW does not support ECMP** \u2014 return traffic always takes one path\\r\\n2. **DX always wins over VPN** at the VGW \u2014 cannot prefer VPN for return traffic\\r\\n3. **Same DX location required for flow-hashing** \u2014 different locations in same region get single-path selection\\r\\n4. **Use unequal LP + AS-path** for active/passive designs to avoid asymmetric routing\\r\\n5. **Asymmetric routing is the primary failure mode** \u2014 designs with equal attributes from multiple CGW devices without synchronization will cause issues\\r\\n6. **MED can influence VGW path selection** \u2014 documented at [VPN route priority](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority.html)\\r\\n'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "a2bd3488-5713-4fff-9b53-7ab2b7ee7a01", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_x0LUu0nkFAEchdsCgz5z5v", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/vpn-route-priority.html\",\"content\":\"# Route tables and AWS Site-to-Site VPN route priority\\n\\nRoute tables determine where\\nnetwork traffic from your VPC is directed. In your VPC route table, you must add a route\\nfor your remote network and specify the virtual private gateway as the target. This\\nenables traffic from your VPC that's destined for your remote network to route via the\\nvirtual private gateway and over one of the VPN tunnels. You can enable route\\npropagation for your route table to automatically propagate your network routes to the\\ntable for you.\\n\\nWe use the most specific route in your route table that matches the traffic to\\ndetermine how to route the traffic (longest prefix match). If your route table has\\noverlapping or matching routes, the following rules apply:\\n\\n* If propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection or Direct Connect connection overlap\\n  with the local route for your VPC, the local route is most preferred even if the\\n  propagated routes are more specific.\\n* If propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection or Direct Connect connection have the\\n  same destination CIDR block as other existing static routes (longest prefix\\n  match cannot be applied), we prioritize the static routes whose targets are an\\n  internet gateway, a virtual private gateway, a network interface, an instance\\n  ID, a VPC peering connection, a NAT gateway, a transit gateway, or a gateway VPC\\n  endpoint.\\n\\nFor example, the following route table has a static route to an internet gateway, and\\na propagated route to a virtual private gateway. Both routes have a destination of\\n`172.31.0.0/24`. In this case, all traffic destined for\\n`172.31.0.0/24` is routed to the internet gateway \u2014 it is a static\\nroute and therefore takes priority over the propagated route.\\n\\n| Destination | Target |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| 10.0.0.0/16 | Local |\\n| 172.31.0.0/24 | vgw-11223344556677889 (propagated) |\\n| 172.31.0.0/24 | igw-12345678901234567 (static) |\\n\\nOnly IP prefixes that are known to the virtual private gateway, whether through BGP\\nadvertisements or a static route entry, can receive traffic from your VPC. The virtual\\nprivate gateway does not route any other traffic destined outside of received BGP\\nadvertisements, static route entries, or its attached VPC CIDR. Virtual private gateways\\ndo not support IPv6 traffic.\\n\\nWhen a virtual private gateway receives routing information, it uses path selection to\\ndetermine how to route traffic. Longest prefix match applies, if all endpoints are\\nhealthy. The health of a tunnel endpoint takes precedence over other routing attributes.\\nThis precedence applies to VPNs on virtual private gateways and Transit Gateways. If the\\nprefixes are the same, then the virtual private gateway prioritizes routes as follows,\\nfrom most preferred to least preferred:\\n\\n* BGP propagated routes from an Direct Connect connection\\n\\n  Blackhole routes are not propagated to a Site-to-Site VPN customer gateway via BGP.\\n* Manually added static routes for a Site-to-Site VPN connection\\n* BGP propagated routes from a Site-to-Site VPN connection\\n* For matching prefixes where each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses BGP, the AS PATH is\\n  compared and the prefix with the shortest AS PATH is preferred.\\n\\n  **Note:**\\n\\n  AWS strongly recommends using customer gateway devices that support\\n  asymmetric routing.\\n\\n  For customer gateway devices that support asymmetric routing, we\\n  *do not* recommend using AS PATH prepending, to\\n  ensure that both tunnels have equal AS PATH. This helps to ensure that the\\n  multi-exit discriminator (MED) value that we set on a\\n  tunnel during VPN tunnel endpoint\\n  updates is used to determine tunnel priority.\\n\\n  For customer gateway devices that do not support asymmetric routing, you\\n  can use AS PATH prepending and Local Preference to prefer one tunnel over\\n  the other. However, when the egress path changes, this may cause traffic to\\n  drop.\\n* When the AS PATHs are the same length and if the first AS in the AS_SEQUENCE\\n  is the same across multiple paths, multi-exit discriminators\\n  (MEDs) are compared. The path with the lowest MED value is preferred.\\n\\nRoute priority is affected during VPN\\ntunnel endpoint updates.\\n\\nOn a Site-to-Site VPN connection, AWS selects one of the two redundant tunnels as the primary\\negress path. This selection may change at times, and we strongly recommend that you\\nconfigure both tunnels for high availability, and allow asymmetric routing. The health\\nof a tunnel endpoint takes precedence over other routing attributes. This precedence\\napplies to VPNs on virtual private gateways and Transit Gateways.\\n\\nFor a virtual private gateway, one tunnel across all Site-to-Site VPN connections on the gateway\\nwill be selected. To use more than one tunnel, we recommend exploring Equal Cost\\nMultipath (ECMP), which is supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on a transit gateway. For\\nmore information, see Transit gateways in\\n*Amazon VPC Transit Gateways*. ECMP is not supported for Site-to-Site VPN connections on\\na virtual private gateway.\\n\\nFor Site-to-Site VPN connections that use BGP, the primary tunnel can be identified by the\\nmulti-exit discriminator (MED) value. {"id": "1bf4b205-f7a5-4949-9fce-0b9dff194d7b", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This confirms the behavior. Here's how it works for your setup:

## Which path AWS prefers (VPC/VGW → on-prem)

For the **same destination prefix**, the VGW prioritizes route sources in this order (highest to lowest):

1. **BGP propagated routes from Direct Connect** ← your DX wins here
2. Manually added static VPN routes
3. BGP propagated routes from Site-to-Site VPN
4. Among VPN BGP routes with matching prefixes, shortest AS-path, then lowest MED

**Bottom line: Direct Connect always wins over VPN for same-prefix return traffic.** This is a fixed VGW preference — you cannot override it with BGP attributes (LP, AS-path, MED) on the VPN side. The only way to force traffic onto the VPN path is to advertise a **more specific (longer) prefix** over the VPN — longest-prefix-match is evaluated *before* the attachment-type preference, so a /24 via VPN beats a /16 via DX for matching traffic.

Also note: **VGW doesn't support ECMP**, so even on the VPN alone, return traffic always rides a single tunnel (the "Preferred Tunnel") — never load-balanced across both tunnels.

## How to avoid asymmetric routing

1. **Make your customer gateway router send on-prem→AWS traffic over DX whenever DX is up.** Since AWS will always return via DX anyway, if your CGW prefers VPN while DX is healthy, you get asymmetric routing (egress on VPN, ingress on DX).
2. **Don't try to prefer VPN over DX using BGP attributes** (LP/AS-path/MED) for the *same* prefix — it won't work; the VGW's attachment-type preference overrides it.
3. **If you genuinely need VPN to carry specific traffic** (e.g., for testing or partial failover), advertise a more-specific prefix over the VPN than what's advertised over DX — that's the one lever that beats the DX preference.
4. **Use a CGW device that explicitly supports asymmetric routing**, per AWS's recommendation — this matters especially during automatic VPN tunnel endpoint maintenance, when AWS may shift the primary VPN tunnel without the health of DX changing.
5. **Treat the VPN purely as passive backup**: it should only carry traffic when DX is fully down (BGP session drops and the DX route disappears), at which point the VGW naturally falls back to the VPN route — no manual intervention needed.

If you want, I can pull the current BGP state of your DX VIF and VPN tunnels (AS-path, advertised prefixes) to confirm they're configured as a clean active/passive pair.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
